terms.gloss: a state: its citizens as one body; one of the United States
evidence: Cic. Amic. 23: quae tam firma cīvitās est
terms.comment: The state as a community of citizens, from a city to a nation. Traupman and Morgan–Owens use it for each of the United States, Cīvitātēs Foederātae (Traupman 180).

terms.grammar: noun, fifth declension, with an adjective
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.54: quasi sēminārium reī pūblicae
terms.comment: The state as everyone’s concern, against private life: sī rē pūblicā nōn possīs fruī, stultum est nōlle prīvātā (Cic. Fam. 4.9.4, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Traupman 180: Ūnītī Statūs, the United States
terms.comment: A false friend: classically a condition, as in status reī pūblicae, the condition of the state, never the state itself (see state, condition).

phrases.latin: quae enim domus tam stabilis, quae tam firma cīvitās est, quae nōn odiīs et discidiīs funditus possit ēvertī?
phrases.english: for what house is so stable, what state so strong, that hatred and quarrels could not overturn it utterly?
How many states does America consist of?

sources: Lewis & Short: civitas · Lewis & Short: res · Lewis & Short: publicus · Lewis & Short: status
